details: RBMK cladding: Zr-1%Nb alloy (Soviet designation E-110); composition: Zr base + 1.0% Nb + trace O + Fe + Cr; OD=13.6mm; wall=0.9mm; length=3.64m; 18 rods per fuel assembly; mechanical: UTS=440 MPa; yield=350 MPa at 20°C (decreasing at operating T=300°C); oxidation threshold: above 900°C: Zr + 2H₂O → ZrO₂ + 2H₂ (ΔH=−602 kJ/mol net exothermic for full ZrO₂ formation); H₂ generation: 1 mol H₂ per mol Zr oxidized; kinetics: parabolic rate law at 900-1200°C: Δx²=A×exp(−Q/RT)×t where Q=167 kJ/mol; transition to rapid linear kinetics above 1200°C; US NRC 10CFR50.46: ECR (equivalent cladding reacted) limit <17% for post-LOCA ductility retention; above ECR limit: brittle fragmentation; RBMK vs Zr-4: E-110 has better corrosion in RBMK low-oxygen water chemistry (no dissolved O₂ in RBMK primary circuit vs PWR high-O primary)
chernobyl_application: ~10 tonnes Zr in RBMK core; theoretical full oxidation → 220 kg H₂ = 5000 m³ at STP; estimated 20-30% reacted during accident → 1000-1500 m³ H₂; hydrogen detonation stoichiometric H₂-air = 29.6% by volume; building confined space → second explosion confirmed by asymmetric blast pattern; ALL cladding failed in <1s (CHF exceeded 200×; prompt criticality); E-110 retained as RBMK standard for operating units; VVER-1000 also uses E-110+ (0.35% Fe addition) for improved corrosion; Westinghouse VVER fuel also uses Zr-1Nb cladding (compatibility requirement for Ukrainian fleet)

details: Nuclear graphite irradiation behavior: hexagonal sp² carbon; a-axis (in-plane C-C) 1.42 Å; c-axis (inter-layer) 3.35 Å; fast neutron (E>0.18 MeV) displacement effects: PKA cascade → Frenkel pairs (vacancy + interstitial carbon); at <300°C: interstitials accumulate between layers → c-axis expansion + a-axis shrinkage → net volume decrease at low fluence; Wigner energy stored: up to 500 J/g (potentially explosive release in uncontrolled anneal); at 280-350°C (RBMK operating): continuous thermal annealing releases Wigner energy safely; dimensional change: initial contraction → turnaround at ~5×10²² n/cm²(E>0.18) → then expansion; turnaround = critical aging threshold; channel bowing: heterogeneous radial flux profile → differential shrinkage across core → Zr channel pipes bow toward high-flux core center → SCRAM rod insertion resistance increases; thermal conductivity degradation: fresh graphite k=100-150 W/m/K → irradiated (5×10²¹ n/cm²) k=30-50 W/m/K (phonon scattering by defects); affects core temperature distribution
chernobyl_application: 5 operating RBMK units (2026): Smolensk-1 (44yr); Kursk-4 (41yr); accumulated fluence ~3-5×10²² n/cm² approaching turnaround zone; Rosatom 2020 safety reports: channel bowing detected; partial graphite block replacement program ongoing; annual eddy current scan of channel pipes for bowing >25mm (limit); 2006 Smolensk-3 incident: 3 columns excessive bowing found → replaced without radiation release; Windscale 1957 contrast: Windscale operated at <150°C → no Wigner annealing → 1957 heating triggered stored energy release → graphite fire; RBMK safe from Wigner fire because operating T (280-350°C) > annealing T; but graphite dust accumulation in channel annuli = secondary concern
source: Burchell 1999 Carbon; Nightingale 1962; IAEA-TECDOC-1340 2003; rbmk_core_neutron_physics_REAL.csv; rbmk_operational_history_REAL.csv

details: UO₂ fission gas behavior: combined Xe+Kr fission yield ~15% (Xe-131 to 136; Kr-84 to 86); volumetric gas generation: ~1.5 cm³(STP)/MWd; at T<1000°C: gas retained in vacancy clusters and intragranular bubbles; at 1000-1600°C: bubble migration to grain boundaries → grain boundary saturation → intergranular release begins (1-5% FGR per cycle); at >1600°C: rapid FGR (>10% per MWd); at >2865°C (UO₂ melting point): complete release; centerline T in RBMK normal operation: ~400-800°C (low power density 5 W/cm³ average) → FGR <0.5%; rim effect at high burnup: U-238 resonance absorption → Pu-239 buildup in 200µm pellet periphery → rim burnup 3-5× average; rim restructuring (HBS: high burnup structure) → nanometer bubbles → increased porosity → concentrates fission gas at rim; RBMK burnup 20-22 MWd/kgU = relatively low → rim effect minimal; internal rod pressure at accident: FP volatile + Xe + Kr → cladding rupture before thermal melt
chernobyl_application: Chernobyl accident: near-complete volatile FP release to coolant circuit in <1s; I-131 release fraction 50-80% of core inventory; Cs-137 release 20-40%; noble gases ~100% (complete failure of all fuel rods in excursion zone); fuel fragmentation: coarse mm-cm fragments (near-field deposition) + condensed sub-micron aerosol (long-range transport to Scandinavia); UO₂+Pu+Cs fused particles found in Swedish filters = direct evidence of temperatures >3000°C (fuel vaporization + condensation); Chernobyl burnup was NOT limiting factor (prompt criticality overwhelmed thermal limits in ms); post-Chernobyl RBMK fuel: hollow pellet design (reduces centerline T); power ramp rate limits implemented
source: Ronchi 1997 J Nucl Mater; Turnbull 2012; fuel_particle_contamination_REAL.csv; source_term_daily_release_REAL.csv

details: Reactor pressure vessel (RPV) steel radiation embrittlement: mechanism: fast neutrons (E>1 MeV) → atomic displacements (dpa); Cu impurity clustering around vacancies → copper-rich precipitates (CRP) → dislocation pinning → yield stress increase → DBTT (ductile-brittle transition temperature) shifts upward; ΔRTNDT (Regulatory Guide 1.99 Rev.2): ΔRTNDT = A×(C_Cu)^0.5×(C_Ni)^0.3×fluence^0.5; high Cu (>0.2%): ΔRTNDT up to +150°C at 40yr; low Cu (<0.05%): ΔRTNDT <30°C; surveillance capsule program: ASTM-compliant specimens in reactor → periodic Charpy testing → verify vs prediction (IAEA SSG-41); pressurized thermal shock (PTS) risk: emergency coolant injection (cold water) + embrittled RPV → brittle fracture risk; NRC limit: RT_PTS <132°C for plates; 149°C for welds; VVER-440 Model V-230 RPVs: higher Ni (1.3%) → faster embrittlement; VVER-1000: low Cu (<0.1%) → moderate shift; VVER-440 Model V-213: improved design (no emergency nozzle penetrations in core zone)
chernobyl_application: RBMK: NO single RPV (distributed design: 1661 individual Zr-2.5Nb pressure tubes each 88mm OD × 4mm wall × 8 MPa); RBMK pressure tube concern: H pickup from corrosion → ZrH₂ hydrides → DHC (delayed hydride cracking); CANDU: same pressure tube design → Pickering-2 1983 pressure tube failure (initiating event); RBMK mitigation: periodic tube replacement every 25-30yr + H measurement; Ukrainian VVER fleet: RPV surveillance programs compliant IAEA SSG-41; VVER-1000 low Cu → moderate embrittlement; Rivne-1 (1980): RPV fluence by 2040 ~2×10¹⁹ n/cm² → ΔRTNDT ~50-70°C (within safety limit); ZNPP VVER-1000 RPV surveillance suspended under Russian occupation (IAEA concern 2023 report)
source: IAEA SSG-41 2021; ASTM E900-15; NUREG/CR-6551; ukraine_nuclear_fleet_REAL.csv; zaporizhzhia_npp_2022_2025_REAL.csv

details: Chernobyl corium physical and chemical properties: formation: ~170-220t (UO₂ + Zr cladding + Zr channel pipes + SiO₂ sand/concrete + graphite + Fe/Ni/Cr steel) at >2000°C → molten lava; bulk composition (Elephant's Foot and basement formations): ~60% UO₂ + ~25% Zr silicate glass + ~8% metal oxides + ~5% graphite + ~2% fission products; density: 7,000-9,000 kg/m³ (heterogeneous; vs pure UO₂=10,970 kg/m³ → silicate matrix reduces density); hardness: >7 Mohs (glassy silicate harder than quartz); thermal conductivity k: 1.5-2.5 W/m/K (reduced from UO₂ 3.6 by vitrification); radioactive decay heat 2026: ~0.4-0.8 W/kg (Cs-137 + Sr-90 + Pu isotopes); total heat from ~170t: ~70-140 kW; NSC passive cooling capacity: natural convection air designed for this load; stability: Zr silicate matrix = geochemically stable borosilicate glass analogue; U leach rate in pH<7 groundwater: very slow (<1 µg/L in contact tests); Am-241 growing in corium (Pu-241 t½=14.29yr → Am-241; peaks 2058.7); increasing alpha dose to corium-adjacent zones
chernobyl_application: Elephant's Foot dose rate: 10,000 R/hr (100 Gy/hr) in 1986 → 34 µSv/hr in 2026 (40yr decay: Cs-137 0.5^(40/30)=40% remaining; Sr-90 same; combined rate drop factor ~3000; + geometry/buildup factor changes); NSC Room 305/2 neutron flux: doubled 2016-2021 (sarcophagus damage → water ingress → neutron moderation increase); STABLE since improved NSC drainage 2022 + NSC closure; no re-criticality risk confirmed by IAEA 2021 (insufficient fissile geometry); Pu content in corium: ~180-200 kg (reactor-grade; Pu-240/Pu-239 ratio ~0.28 = proliferation-unattractive + inaccessible + lethal dose field); no extraction plan; in-situ management for centuries
source: Pazukhin 1994 Radiochem; Anderson 2020 Prog Nucl Energy; corium_fcm_physics_REAL.csv; chernobyl_decommissioning_physics_REAL.csv

details: Radiation effects on concrete: gamma mechanisms: H₂O radiolysis in cement paste → H₂ bubbles + OH radicals; aggregate irradiation: quartz SiO₂ → amorphous metamict state at high gamma → volume expansion → internal microcracking; neutron mechanisms: aggregate lattice displacement → quartz expansion 17% volume → aggregate expansion reaction (AAR analogous); thermal effects: radiolysis heat + radiation heating compounds chemical degradation; dose thresholds: gamma <10 MGy → negligible strength change (<5%); 10-100 MGy → 5-25% strength reduction (microcracking); >200 MGy → 30-60% reduction (structural concern); neutron: >10¹⁸ n/cm² → significant aggregate expansion; typical bioshield concrete over 40yr operation: gamma 1-50 MGy; neutron 10¹⁷-10¹⁸ n/cm² (borderline concern for 60+ yr life); aggregate selection: basalt or limestone better than silica quartz for radiation resistance
chernobyl_application: Chernobyl sarcophagus concrete: 1986 rapid construction (6 months) → air void content 3-8%; measured strength ~18 MPa vs 30 MPa design; near-corium zones received >100 MGy gamma in first decade → estimated 20-40% degradation; carbonation depth measured 2019: 25-35mm (indicating progressive deterioration); NSC concrete design: radiation-resistant basalt aggregate (not silica quartz) for radiation-exposed zones; NSC concrete gamma dose rate: <1 Gy/yr in main structure → <100 Gy over 100yr → negligible degradation; fiber optic strain sensors embedded in NSC concrete → real-time structural health monitoring; seismic design: NSC designed for 0.15g peak ground acceleration (Eastern European reference earthquake)
source: Naus 2010 NUREG/CR-7104; Graves 2016 ACI Mat J; chernobyl_shelter_sarcophagus_REAL.csv; corium_fcm_physics_REAL.csv

details: Fuel cladding failure modes: (1) PCI (pellet-cladding interaction): UO₂ thermal expansion + SCC from I₂ fission product → Zr grain boundary crack propagation; prevention: power ramp rate limits (≤30 W/cm/min); graphite-coated cladding; soft pellets; (2) Fretting: coolant flow turbulence excites fuel rod vibration → wear at spacer grid contacts → wall thinning → perforation; prevention: improved grid-to-rod contact geometry; (3) Creep collapse: external coolant pressure (RBMK 8 MPa) > He fill gas pressure (~2-3 MPa) → slow inward creep → collapse onto pellet stack → mechanical failure; prevention: pellet-cladding clearance minimization; (4) Hydriding: Zr + H (from radiolysis or corrosion) → ZrH₂ precipitates in cladding → delayed hydride cracking (DHC): crack initiates at hydride platelet → stress-corrosion propagation; CANDU Pickering-2 1983: pressure tube DHC rupture = reference event; (5) Corrosion: ZrO₂ layer growth → spallation at >100 µm → accelerated corrosion; RBMK: Zr-1Nb low-corrosion performance adequate; PWR: higher H₂ in coolant to reduce oxidation
chernobyl_application: RBMK fuel failure rate normal operation: <0.1% defective rods per cycle; post-Chernobyl RBMK fuel improvements: hollow fuel pellets (lower centerline T → lower FGR + lower pellet-cladding stress); graphite interlayer discs between pellets; fuel rod gas plenum enlarged; ramp rate limits strictly enforced; Ukrainian VVER + Westinghouse fuel: Zr-1Nb cladding compatible; SCC resistance: Westinghouse uses TREX (two-step pilgering) vs Russian REKS process → slightly different texture → comparable SCC resistance; failure rate in mixed VVER core: <0.05% per cycle; Chernobyl accident: PCI/fretting/creep irrelevant (prompt criticality millisecond timescale overwhelmed all material failure modes)
source: Strasser 2003 ANS; IAEA TECDOC-744; rbmk_fuel_specifications_REAL.csv; ukraine_nuclear_fleet_REAL.csv

details: RBMK graphite aging status (2026): five operating units: Kursk-3 (1978; 48yr); Kursk-4 (1985; 41yr); Smolensk-1 (1982; 44yr); Smolensk-2 (1985; 41yr); Smolensk-3 (1990; 36yr); ALL beyond original 30yr design life; estimated fast neutron fluence: Smolensk-1 ~3.5-4×10²² n/cm²; Kursk-3 ~4-5×10²² n/cm² (approaching dimensional turnaround); safety margins: channel bowing increases SCRAM rod insertion time (normal ~10-15s → bowed ~18-22s; within 30s safety limit); void coefficient: still slightly positive (+1-2 pcm/%void after 1986-1991 modifications; down from +4-8 pcm/%void pre-accident); power tilt limits tightened to prevent hot-channel formation in non-uniform core; Rosatom license extensions: to 2025-2033 (depending on unit); license renewal applications underway for post-2033; replacement: Kursk II (VVER-TOI) Unit-1 construction >90% complete 2026; Smolensk: VVER-TOI feasibility study; commitment: all RBMK offline by 2035
chernobyl_application: IAEA 2021 RBMK peer review (IAEA-TECDOC-1340 updated): residual risks acknowledged (positive void coefficient + graphite aging + no full containment); current safety case accepted with defense-in-depth and improved SCRAM; RBMK = last class of reactor with positive void coefficient operating anywhere in world 2026; global significance: if any RBMK has accident under current configuration → post-Chernobyl analysis showed: SCRAM speed improvement means accident cannot reach 1986 power excursion level; BUT: failure mode = different pathway than 1986 (turbine test configuration + xenon pit + extreme ORM deficit = extremely unlikely to be reproduced); ongoing Rosatom commitment: phase-out by 2035 confirmed in 2022 Russian Energy Strategy
source: IAEA-TECDOC-1340; Rosatom Annual Report 2024; Popov 2010 At Energy; rbmk_operational_history_REAL.csv; rbmk_safety_modifications_REAL.csv
